extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning mathematical proofs / readers of an introductory book on proof and logic
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory chapter-level guidance on the logical language and conventions used in mathematical proofs: what counts as a statement/open sentence, propositional connectives, truth tables, logical equivalences, and quantifiers, with examples and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement is a sentence or a mathematical expression that is either definitely true or definitely false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements are pieces of information that are either correct or incorrect and are the primary objects to which logic is applied. Examples given: 'Every even number is divisible by 2', 'The set {0,1,2} has three elements.' Distinguish statements from non-statements (commands, questions, open sentences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open sentence versus statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence that contains variables whose truth depends on the values of those variables is an open sentence and not a statement (unless variables are instantiated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denote an open sentence by P(x); e.g., Q(x): 'The integer x is even' is not a statement until x is specified. Use notation P(x), P(x,y) to emphasize variables. Examples show when such sentences are true or false for particular values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish correct logic from true information
rubrics_metrics.description: Logic is the process of deducing information correctly, not the same as deducing correct information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An argument can be logically correct even if some premises are false; correctness concerns the valid combination of premises to conclusions. Example: a false premise 'Circle X has radius 3' can still lead by valid inference to a false conclusion, yet the logical steps are correct. Important when exploring consequences of assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use propositional variables as shorthand
rubrics_metrics.description: Designate particular statements by letters P, Q, R, S (with subscripts if needed) as a useful shorthand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simplifies repeated reference to complex sentences (e.g., refer to 'f(x)=x^2 is continuous' as R). Subscripts allow extension to many statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunction ('and', symbol ^)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P and Q are statements, P ^ Q stands for 'P and Q'; P ^ Q is true iff both P and Q are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table provided. Examples of false conjunctions when either conjunct is false. Use ^ to build more complex statements; helper columns useful in truth tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunction ('or', symbol v) — inclusive or
rubrics_metrics.description: If P and Q are statements, P v Q represents 'P or Q' meaning one or both of P and Q is true (inclusive or).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table provided. Explicitly note the mathematical meaning differs from some everyday uses (which may be exclusive). To express 'exactly one', use constructions like (P v Q) ^ ~(P ^ Q), 'Either P or Q', or 'P or Q, but not both.' Examples and exercises demonstrate translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negation ('not', symbol ~)
rubrics_metrics.description: ~P means 'It is not true that P' (the negation of P); ~P is true exactly when P is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table given. Multiple English phrasings for negation listed ('It is false that...', 'The number 2 is not even.'). Note that ~ acts on a single statement and has high precedence when parsing expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional ('if P, then Q', symbol =>)
rubrics_metrics.description: P => Q (read 'If P, then Q' or 'P implies Q') asserts that whenever P is true then Q is true; it is false only when P is true and Q is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table and many equivalent English phrasings are provided ('Q if P', 'P is a sufficient condition for Q', 'P only if Q' etc.). Use examples (professor promise) to illustrate why rows with P false give P=>Q true. Emphasizes precise meaning and common paraphrases in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation as sufficient/necessary conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: P => Q expresses that P is a sufficient condition for Q and Q is a necessary condition for P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains everyday wording versus mathematical usage; gives alternative grammars ('For Q, it is sufficient that P', 'Q is necessary for P'). Useful when analyzing statements and converting everyday language to formal conditional form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive equivalence (useful proof strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: P => Q is logically equivalent to (~Q) => (~P) (the contrapositive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table shown. Noted as useful because proving (~Q) => (~P) may be easier than proving P => Q directly; referenced later chapters on proof techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biconditional ('if and only if', symbol ↔ or ©)
rubrics_metrics.description: P ↔ Q means (P => Q) ^ (Q => P): P if and only if Q; P is a necessary and sufficient condition for Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth table provided. Multiple English formulations listed ('P is equivalent to Q', 'P is necessary and sufficient for Q'). Explains that P ↔ Q is true exactly when P and Q have the same truth value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth tables for compound statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Build truth tables by enumerating all truth-value combinations of component statements and computing intermediate columns as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show method with helper columns for intermediate expressions; examples include two- and three-variable tables and complex combinations like (P v Q) ^ ~(P ^ Q). Notes helper columns are optional once one is confident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical equivalence (same truth table line-for-line)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two statements are logically equivalent if their truth values match line-for-line in a truth table; equivalently they can be interchanged without changing logical content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples and a summarized list of standard equivalences (contrapositive law, DeMorgan's laws, commutative, distributive, associative laws). Emphasizes usefulness for rewriting statements and simplifying proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: DeMorgan's laws
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verified by truth tables and intuitively explained: negation of 'both' means 'at least one is false'. Shows how to extract information quickly (e.g., ~ (P v Q) implies ~P and ~Q). Exercises ask to verify and apply these laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parentheses and operator precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses determine structure; ~ is like unary minus and has high precedence; associative laws allow dropping parentheses for repeated same operator, but parentheses are essential when mixing ^ and v.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ~P v Q means (~P) v Q, not ~(P v Q). You may drop parentheses in PA(QA R) when associativity applies, but must keep them when ^ and v mix because Pv(Q ^ R) differs from (P v Q) ^ R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translating English phrases into logical form
rubrics_metrics.description: Many English constructions correspond directly to logical forms; e.g., 'If P then Q', 'Q if P', 'P is necessary/sufficient for Q', 'P if and only if Q'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text provides a summary list of grammatical variants that mean the same as P => Q and P ↔ Q and includes numerous exercises converting everyday sentences into formal 'If P then Q' or 'P iff Q' forms. Encourages analyzing wording carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusive vs exclusive 'or' and how to express exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical 'or' (v) is inclusive (one or both). To express 'exactly one', use (P v Q) ^ ~(P ^ Q) or other equivalent constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples contrast university official's everyday exclusive use with precise mathematical inclusive meaning. Gives explicit constructions for 'but not both', 'exactly one', and alternatives ('Either P or Q').

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifiers: universal (∀) and existential (∃)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce ∀ ('for all') and ∃ ('there exists') to compactly express infinite conjunctions/disjunctions: e.g., ∀x∈X, P(x) or ∃x∈X, P(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines quantifiers, gives notation variants (Vn ∈ Z, E(2n)), and shows examples (Every integer not odd is even; There exists an integer that is not even). Explains truth conditions: ∀ true iff P(x) true for every x; ∃ true iff P(x) true for some x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier order and scope matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The order and grouping of quantifiers affects meaning (e.g., ∀x ∃y differs from ∃y ∀x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show translations like 'For every real x there is a real y for which y^2 = x' (∀x ∈ R ∃y ∈ R, y^2 = x). Exercises and examples imply and illustrate sensitivity of meaning to quantifier order and domain specification.
